1. Project Background  


SMS spam remains a persistent threat, particularly affecting two vulnerable user groups: younger users, who are more likely to click suspicious links due to overconfidence, and older users, who often lack technical familiarity. With over 5,500 SMS messages labeled as either “spam” or “ham” from the UCI Machine Learning repository, this dataset provides a rich foundation for developing a spam detection model.

The primary goal of this project is to build a robust classifier using transformer-based NLP models (BERT), outperforming traditional frequency-based methods such as TF-IDF. The outcome benefits users by providing an intelligent, real-time spam detection tool deployed via a web interface.

- Suitable for which organization:   
   1. Telcos & Mobile Network Operators: Maxis/CelcomDigi run large-scale “SMS firewalls” that deal with millions of smishes (short for SMS phishing) everyday, important for customer retention.  
      2. Government & Regulators: To protect consumers, and keeping mobile network clean from smishes ([CelcomDigi Help Centre](https://help.celcomdigi.com/support/solutions/articles/70000653010-blocking-of-sms-containing-url-link-personal-details-phone-numbers-and-or-others)) (*CelcomDigi Help | SMS Blocking Guide*, n.d.)  
      3. Banks: Protect customers against fraud and phishing scams, stop using SMS for Two Factor authentication. ([Banks to Stop Using SMS OTP, Malaysia The First to Ban: What’s the Alternative \- IPification](https://www.ipification.com/blog/banks-to-stop-using-sms-otp-malaysia-the-first-to-ban-whats-the-alternative/)) (Cheung, 2023\)  
- Target Users:  
      1. Younger users: due to overconfidence clicks  
      2. Older Users: due to tech-familiarity gap   
- Potential Benefits:  
      1. Minimize losses due to fraud  
      2. Protect companies’ interest

2. Project Objectives  
   1. To identify SMS messages as spam or legitimate (ham) using machine learning techniques. 
   2. To model a spam classifier using transformer-based architectures (e.g., BERT) for contextual understanding.  
   3. To evaluate model performance using metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC.

3. EDA

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) was performed to uncover trends, anomalies, and structural patterns in the data. This included visualizing class imbalance, analyzing message length distributions, and examining word frequencies in spam versus ham messages. Additional features like word and character counts were engineered, and correlation heatmaps and plots were used to assess relationships between variables. EDA provided valuable insights that informed the design and expectations of the modeling phase.

The dataset was loaded using ***pandas***, and EDA steps were carried out as follows:

1. Class Distribution:  
* 4,827 “ham” messages (approx. 87%)  
* 747 “spam” messages (approx. 13%)  
* Imbalanced dataset

2. Message Length:  
* Spam messages are typically longer (analyzed with boxplot, histogram)  
* Median word count higher in spam


3. Word Clouds:  
* “Ham”: friendly, casual words  
* “Spam”: promotional phrases, URLs, financial incentives


4. Correlation & Redundancy Check:  
* No strong multicollinearity  
* t-SNE applied to visualize separation of spam and ham using TF-IDF and BERT embeddings

**Class Distribution**  
The dataset contains 4,827 ham messages (approx. 87.37%) and 747 spam messages (approx. 12.63%), as shown in <a name="nav-fig1"></a> [Figure 1](#figure-1-bar-plot-showing-class-distribution-of-ham-vs-spam-messages) (bar plot) and <a name="nav-fig2"></a>[Figure 2](#figure-2-pie-chart-illustrating-the-percentage-of-ham-and-spam-messages) (pie chart). The class ratio of 0.12633 indicates a strong imbalance. This is critical to address, as it can bias models toward the majority class. As a result, performance was evaluated using metrics beyond accuracy, such as Precision, Recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC, to better assess performance on the minority class (spam).

**Text Structure Analysis**

Message length was analyzed through histograms and boxplots. Spam messages were generally longer, with higher median counts in both characters (<a name="nav-fig3"></a>[Figure 3](#figure-3-histogram-of-message-lengths-by-character-count-for-ham-and-spam-messages)) and words (<a name="nav-fig4"></a>[Figure 4](#figure-4-histogram-of-message-word-counts-for-ham-and-spam-messages)). Spam messages frequently contained 150–200 characters and over 20 words, while ham messages mostly remained under 150 characters and 30 words. Sentence count distribution (<a name="nav-fig5"></a>[Figure 5](#figure-5-histogram-of-sentence-counts-in-ham-and-spam-messages)) showed that ham messages commonly had 1–2 sentences, while spam messages exhibited a broader range, occasionally exceeding 3 sentences. These features suggest spam messages are more detailed and structured, offering useful input for classification.

**Word Usage and Vocabulary**

WordClouds in <a name="nav-fig6"></a>[Figure 6](#figure-6-wordcloud-of-common-terms-in-ham-messages) and <a name="nav-fig7"></a>[Figure 7](#figure-7-wordcloud-of-common-terms-in-spam-messages) provide a visual summary of frequently used terms. Ham messages featured casual, conversational terms like *“ok”*, *“call”*, *“u”*, and *“will”*, while spam messages were dominated by promotional keywords such as *“FREE”*, *“claim”*, *“win”*, and *“text”*. These differences further emphasize the unique linguistic patterns between the two classes.

**Feature Comparison and Correlation**

Boxplots in <a name="nav-fig8"></a>[Figure 8](#figure-8-boxplot-of-character-counts-in-ham-and-spam-messages) and <a name="nav-fig9"></a>[Figure 9](#figure-9-boxplot-of-word-counts-in-ham-and-spam-messages) showed that spam messages have more consistent lengths (narrower IQR) and fewer outliers, while ham messages showed greater variability, likely due to personal writing styles. Despite some overlap, these patterns support the use of length-based features for classification. Correlation analysis in <a name="nav-fig11"></a>[Figure 11](#figure-11-correlation-heatmap-of-message-features-and-class-label) revealed a strong relationship between number of characters and words (0.97), and moderate correlations with sentence count (0.62–0.68). All features showed some correlation with the class label, confirming their relevance for modeling. Importantly, no multicollinearity was detected.

#### **t-SNE Visualizations: TF-IDF vs BERT**

Dimensionality reduction with t-SNE was applied to visualize message clustering based on textual features. The TF-IDF t-SNE plot (<a name="nav-fig12"></a>[Figure 12](#figure-12-t-sne-visualization-of-tf-idf-vectors-for-ham-and-spam-messages)) showed partial separation, with spam messages forming denser clusters in certain regions. Top TF-IDF scores for spam included *“free”*, *“txt”*, *“claim”*, and *“mobile”*, while ham messages featured *“ok”*, *“just”*, and *“come”*—demonstrating vocabulary differences. In contrast, the BERT-based t-SNE plot (<a name="nav-fig13"></a>[Figure 13](#figure-13-t-sne-visualization-of-bert-embeddings-for-ham-and-spam-messages)) revealed clearer separation between spam and ham. Spam messages formed a compact, isolated cluster, while ham messages were more dispersed. This highlights BERT’s strength in capturing deeper semantic meaning and context beyond surface-level word frequency.

4. Data Modelling

   To ensure the quality and consistency of the dataset, several preprocessing steps were undertaken. These steps are crucial in transforming raw text data into a structured format suitable for training and testing.  

   1. **Data Preprocessing:**  
   * Null and Duplicate Values Removal:  
   There were no null// missing messages in the dataset. Duplicate messages which could lead to overfitting or redundancy in machine learning were eliminated.

   * Label Encoding:  
   The dataset originally contained categorical labels: "ham" (0) and "spam."(1) These were converted to numerical format for compatibility with machine learning algorithms:  
   * Text Normalization and Cleaning  
      * Punctuation Removal:  
      Non-alphanumeric characters and punctuation marks were removed using string punctuation, reducing noise and dimensionality in feature space.

      * Stop Words Removal:  
   Commonly used words ("the", "and", "is") were removed using NLTK's predefined list. These words often do not carry significant meaning in classification tasks.

      * Lemmatization:  
   Words were reduced to their base. For example, "running" becomes "run", and "better" becomes "good", helping in reducing word variants and improving model generalization.


   2.  Feature Extraction

  * TF-IDF (Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency):  
     A statistical measure used to evaluate the importance of a word in a document relative to a collection. TF-IDF helps in emphasizing uncommon but potentially meaningful words while down-weighting common words.

  * BERT Embeddings:  
    Leveraged pre-trained BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) embeddings to capture deep contextual and semantic meaning of words within the message. Unlike traditional vectorization methods, BERT considers the context of a word based on surrounding words, allowing the model to better understand nuances and sentence structures. Specifically, we used BERT to extract the CLS (classification) embeddings of the sentence, and it is inferred by all other words in the same sentence, making it a good representation of sentence-level classification. No preprocessing such as stop-word removal, lemmatization was needed for applying BERT as it understands sentences on a contextual level as excessive text cleaning may even worsen the result of BERT outputs (Bricken, 2021).

* **Data Splitting:**

   We implemented a 70-30 train-test split, and a stratified 5-fold cross validation for validation split to tune the models’ hyperparameters, both splitting methods use a fixed seed value of 7001 for reproducible research. Next, the TF-IDF vectorizer was fitted on the test split and transformed both train and test splits to avoid data leakage. The fitted vectorizer is subsequently saved in a .pkl file for web-app vectorizing messages purposes. For the final step, we prepare the data in a tensor type for our deep learning models as well.

* **Model Training:**

   Five model classifiers were developed using ***scikit-learn**, **xgboost, tensorflow libraries*** in Python, namely Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Multinomial Naive Bayes and Multilayer Perceptron, a deep learning model. Based on the t-SNE graphs in EDA and previous studies in the literature reviews, we have decided to apply the modelling techniques: Logistic Regression, SVM, MLP, XGBoost on the **BERT embeddings**, and Logistic Regression, SVM, XGBoost and Multinomial Naive Bayes on the **TF-IDF vectors**.

   * Logistic Regression \- models the probability that an input belongs to a class by fitting a weighted linear combination  
   * SVM \- finds the optimal hyperplane that best separates the two different classes of data by maximizing the margin, kernel hyperparameter can be tuned to handle non-linear boundaries as well.  
   * Multinomial Naive Bayes \- the Naive part comes from the assumption that the independent features are conditionally independent, and the model assumes that the features follow a multinomial distribution and calculates the probability of each class with a cutoff threshold.  
   * MLP \- A type of deep learning model, neural network that learns to map inputs to outputs through layers of hidden neurons, using weighted sums, non-linear activation functions such as ReLu and sigmoid functions, loss functions and optimizer such as Adam to capture complex patterns.  
   * XGBoost \- Builds an ensemble of decision trees in a boosting manner, meaning sequential where each new tree builds on top of the previous ones, correcting the errors using a loss function and optimizer.

* Hyperparameter Tuning:

   For each of the models except MLP, we used the GridSearchCV method in Python to tune for the best hyperpameters.

5. Data Interpretation  
   Performance Metrics:  
   ![evaluation_metrics](images/evaluation_metrics.png)
   Model evaluation was carried out through a comprehensive set of metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. These provide a multi-faceted understanding of each model's performance, particularly in handling class imbalance and minimizing false positives. However, the “best” evaluation metric depends on multiple business knowledge; for example, a false positive (FP) implies the machine classifying a ham message as “spam”, effectively filtering a normal message from the user, which could cause inconvenience to both parties. On the other hand, a false negative (FN) implies the machine classifying a spam message as ham and passing through the spam filtering, and to the user’s phones which is dangerous. In respect to the potential damages/consequences of both types of errors and the imbalance dataset, we will emphasize on the metric that is F1 score, a harmonic mean between precision and recall, focusing on the balance between FP and FN.  
   Overall, comparing F1-score of both TF-IDF and BERT methods, we see a stronger performance in BERT, especially via the SVM model. Furthermore, due to the BERT model trained on a large dictionary corpus, it is less susceptible to overfitting. TF-IDF is a vectorizer that was fitted on the training dataset only, and with the introduction of new types of smishing//spam messages, TF-IDF may not vectorize the message properly which requires a more strict and consistent monitoring of its performance. Thirdly, it is also noteworthy that we do not see a significant difference in F1 score between the default model and the counterpart with its hyperparameters tuned. 

   SVM (BERT):  
* SVM performed the best in terms of F1-score, SVM performs the best when there is a clear decision boundary between the features which can be clearly observed in the t-SNE graph.  
* F1-score: 0.9641, Recall: 0.9592  
* This model will be used to classify the messages in the Streamlit web-app.  

  Logistic Regression (BERT):  
* Logistic regression (LR) is a close runner up in F1-score compared to powerhouse models such as MLP and XGBoost. LR performs better when the features are linearly separable. 
* F1-score: 0.9618, Recall: 0.9643  
  Multinomial Naive Bayes (TF-IDF):  
* A probabilistic classifier that works well with TF-IDF from literature studies.  
* F1-score: 0.9301, Recall: 8827  

  SVM (TF-IDF):  
* Similarly, SVM was used in many literature studies that classified SMS Spam using TF-IDF vectorizer.  
* F1-score: 0.9155, Recall: 8571  

  Confusion Matrix Insights:  
* All models showed high true positives (TP) and true negatives (TN).  
* Logistic Regression and XGBoost had the lowest false positives (FP), which is critical in avoiding disruption to legitimate users.  
  ROC-AUC Interpretation:  
* Both Logistic Regression and XGBoost achieved AUC values of 0.99, indicating almost perfect discrimination capability.  
* SVM and Naive Bayes showed slightly lower AUC but still within acceptable thresholds for practical use.  
  In conclusion, SVM with BERT embeddings emerged as the most powerful model, outperforming the TF-IDF vectors. The other models provided useful baselines and comparison points for assessing trade-offs between complexity and performance.

6. Plan for Reproducible Research (Sherene)

To ensure that this SMS spam detection study is replicable and transparent, purposeful precautions were taken throughout the research process. Several best practices have been applied throughout the development process. 

Firstly, all sources of randomness inside the project have been thoroughly controlled to provide consistent and repeatable results over several runs. This is accomplished by incorporating fixed random seeds into the data processing and model training operations. The random\_state argument, which is commonly set to a constant value such as 42, is used consistently in crucial methods such as train\_test\_split() to ensure that the train-test splits are equal in each run.

Git is used to version-manage the project, which is publicly hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/RichieMonkeyNinja/sms-spam. Version control is crucial to guaranteeing the transparency and traceability of the research workflow. Git records every change to the codebase as a commit, providing a thorough history of development that others may use to understand how the project changed over time. This also makes it simple to revert to previous versions if necessary, ensuring that studies may be reproduced exactly as they were originally performed. All project components, including preprocessing scripts, model training and assessment logic, saved model files, and Jupyter notebooks, are meticulously organized and committed on a regular basis.  

Additionally, to allow other researchers to replicate our project, we have created a Google CoLab project online that comes pre-installed with the packages necessary where the users can run the file immediately allowing them to replicate every steps of the code easily.

7. Deployment of Data Product (Richie)  

   A **Streamlit Web App** was developed to simulate a real-world deployment scenario:  
   * **Interface**: User inputs SMS text  
   * **Backend**: BERT + SVM Model // Fitted TF-IDF vectorizer + Multinomial Naive Bayes  
   * **Output**: Real-time classification (“Spam” or “Not Spam”) with probability score  

  The app demonstrates how machine learning models can be used interactively and effectively in detecting malicious SMS content. The interface of the app can be found in <a name="nav-fig14"></a>[Figure 14](#figure-14-interface-of-the-streamlit-web-application),  [SMS Spam Classification](https://sms-spam-richie.streamlit.app/) is the URL link to access the spam classification app where users are encouraged to type a message and see both BERT Embeddings \+ SVM and TF-IDF \+ Multinomial Naive Bayes in action classifying the users’ messages and showing the confidence of that prediction as well. The app followed a beginner-friendly user interface, replicating an AI agent-user conversation format. Furthermore, links are available on the left tab of the app, which sends users to a page explaining BERT and TF-IDF, and another link sends users to the source code of this project in GitHub.

Deployment via Streamlit Cloud are as below:

   1) Create a GitHub repository and push your project folder inside the repo via a command or upload. The project folder must include a requirements.txt, a file with .py extension that contains your streamlit code, and other relevant files such as a .py file that contains declared functions, several .pkl files that contain pre-trained models.

      

   2) requirements.txt is a simple .txt file containing the modules that needs to be installed to run the main python script.

      

   3) Function.py is a .py file that declares functions that will be used in the main streamlit .py file. A Function.py file is not mandatory, but it is usually considered best practice for writing a clean coding script.

      

   4) Once the repo is set-up, we set-up an account in [https://streamlit.io/cloud](https://streamlit.io/cloud) with our GitHub account and select the “Create app” option, then select “Deploy a public app from GitHub”.

      

   5) Enter the relevant repositories, branch, main file path, and an optional relevant App URL.

### 8. Insights and Conclusion (Sherene)

   ### **Key Insights:**

One of the project's most noteworthy findings is that BERT-based representations outperform traditional TF-IDF features. While TF-IDF may detect term frequency and some contextual significance, it lacks the deep semantic knowledge required for sophisticated text classification. In contrast, BERT embeddings, which are pre-trained on large corpora utilizing transformer-based architecture, encode rich contextual associations between words. This semantic depth enables even simple classifiers to produce more accurate predictions when fed BERT embeddings.

Another interesting insight is the structural consistency discovered in spam communications. These messages are usually longer and contain exaggerated language, advertising slogans, and multiple mentions of monetary incentives or urgent calls to action. Advanced models can use this linguistic pattern to increase classification accuracy via feature engineering or attention techniques.

Furthermore, the experiment demonstrates that lightweight machine learning models, such as Logistic Regression, can perform well when combined with sophisticated feature representations like BERT embeddings. It emphasizes the idea that high prediction accuracy does not always necessitate complicated or deep architectures as long as the input features are rich and semantically relevant, simpler models can produce excellent results with less overhead.

However, we believe the line between spam and ham messages in the real world is much more complicated and spam messages are constantly evolving to avoid the SMS firewall. Hence, one of the limitations of this study is an older and imbalanced dataset, with only 13% of a 5000-messages dataset being spam, and up-to-date SMS messages with more spam messages would help generalize the model better, avoiding overfitting and resulting in a better performance. The messages were also extracted from Singapore, with their  Singlish typing styles, such as abbreviating many text such as “you” to “u”, “where” to “whr” and informal words or colloquialisms such as “walao”, which proved to be very difficult to clean. The feature extractions and machine learning models may have focused on these words to classify “spam” or “ham”, which might lead to overfitting. Next, the dataset was also lacking metadata, such as caller location, caller registration date which are vital features for a model to classify the messages. Last but not least, complicated methods such as Deep Learning or Transformers could also be further explored to potentially obtain a better result in SMS spam detection.

### **Conclusion:**

This project successfully built and deployed a high-performing SMS spam detection model. By integrating modern NLP techniques and ensuring reproducibility and accessibility through a Streamlit web app, this solution is practical, scalable, and beneficial to diverse user groups vulnerable to SMS scams.

The end-to-end pipeline, from business understanding to model inference, was built with a strong emphasis on reproducibility, incorporating practices such as fixed random seeds, version-controlled code, reusable pipelines, and model serialization. Additionally, the integration of a Streamlit web application enhances usability by allowing real-time SMS classification through an interactive interface. This makes the tool not only effective but also user-friendly and accessible to non-technical users.

Overall, the approach is practical and scalable, with real-world applications in assisting users, particularly vulnerable individuals and organizations to protect themselves from SMS-based phishing and scam efforts. The project lays the groundwork for future improvements, such as multilingual support, real-time deployment on mobile platforms, and the inclusion of new capabilities like sender verification and message history analysis.
